cl_alc_nac_hangover.q: Do N-acetylcysteine (NAC) pills stop a hangover?
cl_alc_nac_hangover.short: It hasn't been shown. In a trial, 49 young adults drank beer twice, once with NAC and once with dummy pills. Next morning, hangovers weren't clearly different.
cl_alc_nac_hangover.but: It's one small trial, and it couldn't rule out a real effect. Drinking after people went home wasn't checked.
how: 49 healthy adults, mostly white and in their twenties, drank beer twice under watch at a US hospital. In random order, they took NAC once and look-alike dummy pills once. Neither they nor the staff knew which was which.

Next morning, the middle hangover score was 10 with NAC and 13 with dummy pills, on a scale from 0 to 52. A gap that size could easily be chance. Headache, nausea and weakness didn't clearly differ either.
Women's scores were 3.5 points lower on NAC than on dummy pills, and men's 2 points higher. That was one of several comparisons not corrected for chance, so it needs a trial designed to test it.

Side effects were few and mild with both. After NAC there were 4 cases of gut trouble, 2 of headache, and one each of rash, muscle twitches and poor sleep; after dummy pills, 3 of headache and 1 of gut trouble.
cl_alc_nac_hangover.rate: One small trial that gave only middle scores, with no margin of error, so a real effect can't be ruled out. It tested low doses at one timing, and drinking after people left wasn't controlled.

cl_alc_water_dehydration.q: Is a hangover just being thirsty, and does drinking water fix it?
cl_alc_water_dehydration.short: It seems not. Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. Up to mid-2024, no experiment had tested water as a fix.
cl_alc_water_dehydration.but: It all comes through one review, partly its authors' second look at their own data. None of it tested what water does.
how: A 2024 review found no experiment, up to July 2024, that tested if water stops or eases a hangover.

On a long walk in Crete, 176 people with a hangover said how much water they drank. Those who drank more had worse hangovers, but the amount wasn't linked to how much their hangover or thirst changed over the day. The review's authors re-analysed this from their own data.
In surveys of Dutch students, water was the most used hangover remedy. They rated how well it worked at about 5 to 6 out of 10, with nothing to compare it against.

After a night of heavy drinking, people were clearly thirstier than on a day without alcohol only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. Small old studies found mild, brief changes in body fluids. So the authors see being dried out and a hangover as two separate effects of drinking.
cl_alc_water_dehydration.rate: It's all from one review: a walk in the heat where people who felt worse drank more water, students' own ratings, and small, old lab studies of men. No experiment tested water itself.

cl_alc_protective_strategies.q: Do habits meant to make drinking less harmful help?
cl_alc_protective_strategies.short: Nobody knows yet. No trial tested one habit alone. And teaching students a bundle of them barely changed how they said they drank.
cl_alc_protective_strategies.but: Nearly all were US college students. And every result is what they said about themselves.
how: A 2026 review pooled 15 trials, published 2007 to 2023, that taught or prompted bundles of habits like keeping track of drinks, pacing or eating. 13 were at US universities, nearly all with students aged 18 to 24. Most programs were short and digital, often mixed with other parts.

Compared with surveys alone, education or other programs, how much students said they drank didn't clearly change. They drank a tiny bit less often. They may have had a tiny bit fewer alcohol problems, but that could be chance.

A 2013 review of 62 studies says that students who reported more habits nearly always also reported drinking less or fewer problems. But most asked about both at one sitting. In one experiment, students told to use more habits said they did, yet didn't drink less.

In two day-by-day studies, students drank less on days they used habits about how they drank, like pacing, but more on days they used habits for limiting or stopping. On days with a designated driver or a friend to go home with, they drank more and had more problems. The author thinks people plan those for heavy nights.
cl_alc_protective_strategies.rate: The trials agree, but 14 of 15 had weaknesses, every result was self-reported, and nearly all were US students. Habits were taught in bundles, often with other parts, so no single habit was tested.

cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.q: Does loperamide help with opioid withdrawal?
cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.short: We can't say yet. The one study we read counted 26 people seen by poisons doctors after taking it. Six took it to avoid withdrawal; nobody recorded if it helped.
cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.but: It only counted people who saw a poisons doctor. And it had no group to compare them with.
how: A US registry gathered 26 people seen by poisons doctors after taking loperamide, from 2010 or 2011 to 2016. Six of them had taken it to avoid opioid withdrawal.
The records list the problems that brought people to care, not whether withdrawal eased. Results for the six weren't given on their own, and no one was compared with people who didn't take it.
The authors write that people use loperamide to ease withdrawal on their own. They think a lack of methadone or buprenorphine treatment may play a part, but the study didn't measure that.
cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.rate: One small registry of people who needed a poisons doctor. It never measured whether withdrawal eased, and it had no one to compare with.

alcohol.statement: NAC pills have been shown to stop hangovers.
alcohol.why: In the one trial, 49 young adults' next-morning hangovers weren't clearly different on NAC than on dummy pills. One small trial can't rule out an effect, either.

alcohol.statement: A hangover is just being dried out, so drinking water fixes it.
alcohol.why: Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, while the hangover lasted all day. And up to mid-2024, no experiment had tested water as a fix.

alcohol.statement: Trials show that teaching students safer drinking habits cuts how much they drink.
alcohol.why: In 15 trials, mostly with US students, how much they said they drank didn't clearly change. No trial tested one habit alone.

alcohol.statement: Students drank more on days they had a designated driver.
alcohol.why: In two day-by-day studies, they drank more and had more problems on those days. The author thinks people plan a ride home for heavy nights.
